title: Determiners and articles
keyIdea: A determiner is a little word that comes before a noun. a, an and the are called articles. Use an before a word that starts with a vowel sound (an apple, an hour) and a before any other sound (a ball, a unicorn): listen to the sound, not the letter. Use a for any one thing and the for one thing we both know. this and that point at one thing: this is near, that is far. these and those point at many things: these are near, those are far.
familyTip: Play 'near and far' at home. Put one toy by your child and one across the room, then two of each. Ask 'Which one?' and let them answer with this, that, these or those. At snack time, ask 'a apple or an apple?' and let them say both out loud to hear which is easier.

visual.caption: Does each word need a or an? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: a or an by sound, tricky hour and unicorn, a or the, and this, that, these, those near and far.

kid: Some small words go just before a noun. They tell us which one, or how many. They are called determiners. a, an and the are the ones you use the most.

Say the next word out loud. Does it start with a vowel sound, like a, e, i, o or u? Then use an: an apple, an egg, an owl. If it starts with any other sound, use a: a ball, a cat. Your ears decide, not your eyes. We say an hour, because the h is silent. We say a unicorn, because it starts with a you sound.
Use a when any one will do: can I have a biscuit? Use the for one thing we both know about: the sun, or the dog I just told you about.
Point at one thing near you and say this. Point at one thing far away and say that. For lots of things near you, say these. For lots of things far away, say those.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. In the US, Common Core L.1.1h asks first graders to use determiners, both articles (a, an, the) and demonstratives (this, that, these, those). In England, English Appendix 2 lists a or an by the next sound in Year 3 (a rock, an open box) and the term determiner in Year 4, so at this age the aim is correct use, not the label.

The rule for a and an follows speech. an goes before a vowel sound, so an hour and an honest boy, but a uniform and a one-way street, because those start with a y or w sound. The four demonstratives carry two pieces of information at once: distance (near or far from the speaker) and number (one or many). Children often get one right and the other wrong, so the lab checks both.

Common mistakes: choosing by the first letter rather than the first sound (an unicorn, a hour); saying a apple because the rule is not yet heard; using this or that with plural nouns (this shoes, that birds); mixing up near and far; and using a for a thing that is already known (I saw a dog. A dog barked). Say the words out loud together; the easier one to say is usually the right one.

practice.prompt: Which one is right for apple?
practice.hint: Say apple out loud. Does it start with a vowel sound?
practice.explain: apple starts with the vowel sound a, so it is an apple. a apple is hard to say.

practice.prompt: Mia has {n} shells in her hand. What does she say?
practice.hint: The shells are in her hand, so they are near. Is it one shell or many?
practice.explain: Many things near you are these. this is only for one thing, and those are far away.

practice.prompt: Which one is right for unicorn?
practice.hint: Say unicorn slowly. What sound do you hear first?
practice.explain: unicorn starts with a you sound, not a vowel sound, so it is a unicorn, even though it starts with the letter u.

practice.prompt: Sam sees {n} kites far away in the sky. What does he say?
practice.hint: Are the kites near or far? Is it one or many?
practice.explain: Many things far away are those. these are near, and that is for one thing.

practice.prompt: I saw a dog at the park. ___ dog was very big.
practice.hint: Do we already know which dog?
practice.explain: We already know which dog: the one at the park. So it is the dog.

pool.prompt: Which one is right for egg?
pool.hint: Say egg out loud. Listen to the first sound.
pool.explain: egg starts with the vowel sound e, so it is an egg. In an big egg the next word is big, so it would be a big egg.

pool.prompt: Which one is right for hour?
pool.hint: Do you hear the h in hour?
pool.explain: The h in hour is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound: an hour. You can hear the h in horse, so it is a horse.

pool.prompt: One cup is next to you. Which do you say?
pool.hint: Near or far? One or many?
pool.explain: One thing near you is this cup. that is for far away, and these is for many.

pool.prompt: One bird is far away on a roof. Which do you say?
pool.hint: Near or far? One or many?
pool.explain: One thing far away is that bird. this is near, and those is for many.

pool.hint: Which word is only for one thing?
pool.explain: shoes means more than one, and this is only for one thing. Use these shoes or those shoes.

pool.prompt: Can I have ___ biscuit, please? Any one will do.
pool.hint: Any one will do. Does biscuit start with a vowel sound?
pool.explain: Any biscuit is fine, so use a, not the. biscuit starts with a b sound, so it is a, not an.

pool.hint: How many moons do we see in the sky?
pool.explain: There is only one moon, so we both know which one: the moon.

pool.prompt: Which word is a determiner in 'those red apples'?
pool.hint: Which word points at the apples and tells you where they are?
pool.explain: those points at the apples and says they are far away and many. red describes them, and apples is the noun.

pool.prompt: There are {n} crayons by your feet. Pass me ___ crayons.
pool.hint: By your feet is near. Is it one or many?
pool.explain: Many things near you are these crayons. those would be far away, and this is for one thing.

pool.prompt: Dad points at {n} cows far across the field. What does he say?
pool.hint: Far across the field is far away. Is it one cow or many?
pool.explain: Many things far away are those cows. these would be near Dad, and that is for one cow.
